findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. This part works well.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The only section that would show Athena's main promise (models, verdict, cost) is broken, and it shows an internal error message to the public. A newcomer sees a failure instead of proof.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This is Athena's home page, but the title and almost all of the body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer has to read the third paragraph of the lede to learn why that is.
findings.source: title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: What to do next is clear. It is linked from the top and set out as concrete steps with prerequisites and a first command to try.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and Next steps: "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" ... "./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The prerequisites do not say whether a paid model account or API key is needed. They also do not say whether a Rust toolchain is installed for you, even though the lede says Athena is written in Rust. A newcomer can't judge the cost of trying it.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: This link is meant for the site owner. Placed at the top of a public landing page, it confuses a newcomer, who has no proposals.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The firstmate study is careful and traces each statement to a claim. But a newcomer who came to learn about Athena will not use most of it: twelve transition cards, forty-five claims and a long glossary. It shows that Athena is thorough without showing what using Athena is like.
findings.source: States of a piece of work / Transitions / Claims and sources

findings.text: Terms are defined twice on purpose, which makes the page longer. Some definitions also admit they are empty, for example "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope." That is honest, but it adds reading without adding understanding.
findings.source: Words used first: "Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary at the end of the page."
